sections.title: Basic Concept of Articles
sections.content: Articles are small words placed before a noun to clarify its identity. In English, there are three articles: A, An, and The. 'A' and 'An' are indefinite articles, while 'The' is the definite article.

sections.title: Use of A and An
sections.content: Step 1: Identify the sound of the noun (the sound is important, not the letter). Step 2: If the word begins with a vowel sound (like a, e, i, o, u), use 'an'. Step 3: If the word begins with a consonant sound, use 'a'. Example: 'an hour' is correct because the 'h' is silent. 'a university' is correct because the sound begins with 'yu'.

sections.title: Basic Use of 'The'
sections.content: Step 1: Check whether the noun is specific or known. Step 2: Use 'the' before unique objects (sun, moon, earth). Step 3: Use 'the' with superlatives (best, tallest, biggest). Example: 'The sun rises in the east.'

sections.title: Type 0 Conditional (General Truth)
sections.content: Step 1: Identify the 'if' clause. Step 2: Use Simple Present tense in the if-clause. Step 3: Use Simple Present tense in the main clause as well. This structure is used for general truths or scientific facts. Example: 'If you heat water, it boils.'

sections.title: Type 1 Conditional (Real Future Possibility)
sections.content: Step 1: Identify the 'if' clause. Step 2: Use Simple Present tense in the if-clause. Step 3: Use 'will/can/may + base verb (V1)' in the main clause. This structure describes a real or possible future situation. Example: 'If it rains, we will stay at home.'

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: 1. Using 'an' by looking only at the vowel letter even when the sound is consonant. 2. Omitting the article with a specific noun. 3. Using 'will' in the if-clause. 4. Using incorrect tense combinations in conditional sentences.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: A/An depend on the sound of the word, not the letter. 'The' is used for specific or unique things. Type 0 conditionals express general truths, while Type 1 conditionals express real future possibilities.

tricks.title: Remember the Sound Rule
tricks.explanation: Choose the article based on the sound, not the spelling.

tricks.title: Vowel Sound Shortcut
tricks.explanation: If the word starts with a vowel sound, use 'an'.

tricks.title: Unique Object Rule
tricks.explanation: Use 'the' for objects that are unique in the world.

tricks.title: If + Present Shortcut
tricks.explanation: In conditionals, the if-clause uses present tense.
tricks.example: If you work hard, you will succeed.

tricks.title: Zero Conditional Identification
tricks.explanation: If both clauses use present tense, it expresses a general truth.
tricks.example: If you mix red and blue, you get purple.

tricks.title: Will Rule
tricks.explanation: The future result appears in the main clause, not in the if-clause.
tricks.example: If it rains, we will cancel the match.

tricks.title: Meaning Check
tricks.explanation: Read the sentence and determine whether it describes a general truth or a future possibility.
tricks.example: If water freezes, it becomes ice.
